claims.text: The initial single-crystal FeNiCrMn alloy has an FCC structure.
The initial material is free of precipitates, grain boundaries, and high dislocation densities.
Yielding is initiated predominantly by thermally activated dislocation nucleation and glide on {111} planes.
Fe-rich FCC HEAs have low stacking-fault energy that strongly influences yielding.
Severe lattice distortion creates a high Peierls barrier for screw-dislocation motion in the alloy.
Partial dislocations are the dominant mobile carriers, and their motion is controlled by thermally activated crossing of local energy barriers rather than viscous drag.
Dislocation drag dominates the high-rate response of traditional metals.
At cryogenic temperatures, deformation-twin nucleation becomes a primary yielding mode because thermal activation is suppressed.
At cryogenic temperatures, FCC-to-HCP martensitic transformation becomes a primary yielding mode.
At elevated temperatures up to 600 K, thermal energy unlocks Lomer-Cottrell locks and stacking-fault networks, enabling easier glide and reducing strain-rate sensitivity.
Weak strain-rate sensitivity results from a transition from thermally activated glide at low rates to defect-controlled nucleation of new dislocations at higher rates.
Increasing temperature reduces yield stress by unlocking Lomer-Cottrell locks while maintaining ductility without pronounced thermal softening.
The strain-rate sensitivity exponent of FeNiCrMn will be less than 0.02.
Traditional FCC metals have strain-rate sensitivity exponents of approximately 0.05-0.1.
Yield strength will be highest at 77 K.
At 77 K, a significant fraction of deformation will be accommodated by twinning and martensitic transformation.
At 600 K, yield strength will be 20-30% lower than at room temperature.
At 600 K, deformation will be dominated by dislocation glide and partial unlocking of dislocation locks.
The [111] orientation will have the highest yield strength, whereas [001] will have the lowest.
The higher predicted yield strength of [111] is caused by its requiring the maximum number of active slip systems for plasticity.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis initially identifies thermally activated dislocation nucleation and glide as the dominant onset mechanism, but later states that twins and martensitic transformation are the primary yielding modes at low temperature.
The mechanism says thermal activation is insufficient at cryogenic temperature, whereas the falsification rule groups thermal activation together with TRIP/TWIP as dominant cryogenic mechanisms.

The material is described as pristine and free of major defect populations, yet the proposed rate-insensitive regime is said to be controlled by nucleation at defects without identifying which defects remain available.
